title: Encapsulation
objective: Keep an object's data behind its methods, so the object can enforce its own rules.

sources.title: Python tutorial, Classes: Private Variables (the underscore convention)
Python docs: property() (keep attribute syntax but run code on access)
David L. Parnas, On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules (Communications of the ACM 15(12), 1972): information hiding

simplifies: Python has no truly private fields; a leading underscore is a convention that says "don't touch", and property() can add checks while keeping attribute syntax. Real accounts also need locking when two withdrawals happen at once.

steps.caption: An Account with a public balance. The ATM and transfers subtract from it directly.
Nothing in Account stops the balance going below zero. Every caller has to remember to check first.

predict.prompt: The balance is ₹300 and the ATM runs acct.balance -= 500. What stops it?

options.explanation: Right. The data is open, so the account can't protect its own rule.
Python happily stores a negative number.
Account has no code that runs when balance changes, so it can't refuse.

steps.caption: Encapsulate: make the balance non-public (an underscore, by Python convention) and add withdraw(), which holds the rule.
Callers now ask the account to act: acct.withdraw(500). The rule lives in one place, so no caller can forget it.
The underscore is a promise, not a lock: the Python docs say _balance "should be treated as a non-public part of the API".

predict.prompt: Can code outside the class still read acct._balance?

options.text: Yes; the underscore is a convention that says "don't"
options.explanation: Right. Python trusts programmers; the underscore marks it as an implementation detail that may change.
Only names with two leading underscores get renamed (name mangling), and even those can be reached.

options.text: Only code in the same file
options.explanation: Python has no file-level privacy for attributes.

steps.caption: The payoff: every change to the data goes through methods the class controls, so its rules hold however many callers it has.

exercise.change: Accounts may now go down to −₹1,000 (an overdraft).
exercise.hint: Where does the "never below zero" check live in this design?

options.text: Make the balance non-public and give Account a withdraw() that holds the rule
options.explanation: Right. The rule moves into the class that owns the data, so changing it is one edit.

options.text: Write the new limit in a comment above balance
options.explanation: Comments don't run. Every caller would still need its own check.

options.text: Add a shared constant OVERDRAFT = 1000 that every caller uses
options.explanation: Better than three numbers, but each caller still has its own check, and a new rule (say, per-customer limits) means editing all three again.

exercise.explain: The rule now lives with the data it protects. ATM, Transfer and BillPay just call withdraw(), so the overdraft change is one edit to Account, and a new caller can't forget the rule.

quiz.prompt: Why hide a field behind methods?

options.text: So the object can enforce its own rules, and every change goes through one place
options.explanation: Right. That is what makes the object trustworthy, however many callers it has.

options.text: It makes the code run faster
options.explanation: A method call is, if anything, slightly slower; the gain is correctness.
Python allows them; hiding is a design choice.

quiz.prompt: Which method best keeps Account encapsulated?

options.explanation: Right. It says what the caller wants and lets the account check the rule.
A setter that accepts any value is a public field with extra steps.
Handing out the internal data lets callers change it behind the account's back.
